card.hook: The hardest part of photographing Bettys isn't the building, it's the people strolling through your shot while you try to look casual. Good news: the square gives you room to wait them out.
card.stand_here: Stand out in St Helen's Square, across the square from the Bettys corner frontage, and face the corner so the window and front fill the middle of your screen. Sometimes Mansion House peeks out behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the corner window and the whole front. If you can't step back far enough, tap 0.5x to squeeze in more of the square. Want a closer look at the window? Try 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the corner of the building up with a vertical line, then keep your phone level so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Queues can build at busy times and block the view, so be ready to wait a minute for a gap. After dark the lit corner window becomes the star, so try night mode and hold your phone steady against your body.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, try 0.5x so more of the background squeezes in, and put the building over your shoulder. Pick a spot with a little space behind you so it doesn't get lost.
card.rules_and_safety: Please keep the doorway clear for people queuing.
card.challenge: Take five quick shots and pick the one with the cleanest gap in the foreground. Bonus points if nobody's mid-stride.
card.good_to_know: Bettys is the tea room on the corner of St Helen's Square in the middle of York. From some angles Mansion House shows up behind, which helps show it's a proper city-centre square. Turn your phone sideways if you want more of the square and the buildings around it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand out in St Helen's Square, across the square from the Bettys corner frontage, and face the corner so the window and front fill the middle of your screen. Sometimes Mansion House peeks out behind.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a standing position for a selfie with Bettys behind, or a spot for a passer-by to photograph a visitor with the whole building in frame, so I have left both fields empty rather than guess. Sources give only the address: 6-8 St Helen's Square, York YO1 8QP (Free City Guides review, https://www.free-city-guides.com/york/bettys-tea-rooms/; Yelp, https://www.yelp.co.uk/biz/bettys-cafe-tea-rooms-york). Wanderlog's 'best photo spots in York' list includes Bettys at Helen's Square (https://wanderlog.com/list/geoCategory/160490/-best-photo-spots-in-york), but it gives no viewpoint. The York Selfie Trail (https://visityork.org/selfie-trail) and the York Museums Trust trail page (https://www.yorkmuseumstrust.org.uk/news-media/latest-news/visitors-offered-ten-of-yorks-most-iconic-selfie-locations-with-new-online-interactive-map/) do not include Bettys. Results for 'Bettys Parliament Street' were about the Harrogate branch, which I excluded. No page I found states selfie stick or tripod rules, and none gives a safety point for this spot. Checking the spot on the ground, or with a local photo guide, would be the next step.

card.hook: Picture a street where the houses lean in so far they almost whisper to each other across the cobbles. That's the Shambles, and the sky shrinks to a thin strip overhead.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, slightly north of where Little Shambles used to join the street. Turn to face south down the lane so the leaning buildings close in on both sides and lead the eye away from you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which shows the lane much as your eye sees it. Go to 0.5x if the crowds stop you stepping back, or zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to squeeze the leaning upper floors closer together.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the street, then slide it a touch darker so the bright strip of sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Go before 9am or after dark for a clear view of the lane, because it's busiest from mid-morning to late afternoon in summer. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or your chest to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand in Kings Square and face King's Court, with the Shambles behind you over your shoulder. York's official selfie trail names this as the best angle. Use your front camera and hold it a bit lower so the crooked buildings fit in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand where the Shambles meets King's Square, back far enough to fit the whole street and its crooked buildings in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography in the Shambles is unrestricted. The cobbles are uneven, which matters for prams and wheelchairs, so nearby Pavement and King's Square offer flatter routes. Watch your footing while you hold up your phone.
card.challenge: Find a meat hook still hanging outside a shopfront and get a close-up of it, with the shelf below in the shot.
card.good_to_know: Many of the buildings date from roughly 1350 to 1475, so the street keeps a lot of its original medieval building fabric. The name comes from an Old English word for a butcher's bench or stall. In 1885 there were thirty-one butchers' shops here, and the last one closed in the early twentieth century.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, slightly north of where Little Shambles used to join the street. Turn to face south down the lane so the leaning buildings close in on both sides and lead the eye away from you.

card.hook: Picture two huge stone towers, a row of carved doorways, and a lunchtime crowd all trying to get the same shot. York Minster is that kind of place, so a little planning helps.
card.stand_here: Stand in Minster Yard, the open ground in front of the main entrance, and face the west front so both towers fit in one frame. If you're on the side streets, it's a short walk round the building to get there.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front and both towers in, then try 1x for a more natural look. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the carved doorways and tower tops, so take one wide shot and one close one.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or early evening is easiest, with fewer people and low light that brings out the stonework. Guides differ on the perfect time, so check how it looks on the day.
card.selfie_here: Pose beside the Constantine statue with the Minster behind you, which is a spot York Museums Trust picks for group selfies. Or try Precentor's Court, down the narrow alley on the right after the main entrance: walk a few steps in, turn to face the Minster, and use the front camera with the towers over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the grass in Dean's Park, the garden just north of the Minster, so they can frame you with the full towering front behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Minster is still a working church, so stay out of the way of people going in and out and keep your voice and movements considerate. Traffic on Museum Street makes clear shots hard. If you try Duncombe Place, shoot from the pavement or wait for a gap in the traffic.
card.challenge: Can you get both towers dead straight on the gridlines, then a close-up of one carved doorway, and tell which looks better?
card.good_to_know: The first church on this site was recorded in 627, but most of what you see today went up between 1220 and 1472. The two western towers came last, between 1433 and 1472. Inside, it keeps most of its medieval stained glass, and its east window is said to be the largest expanse of medieval glass in the world.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Minster Yard, the open ground in front of the main entrance, and face the west front so both towers fit in one frame. If you're on the side streets, it's a short walk round the building to get there.

card.hook: Where else can you stand next to a record-breaking steam engine, then turn around and find a Japanese bullet train? The National Railway Museum packs big, bold, colourful machines close together, so almost every direction you point your phone gives you a good shot.
card.stand_here: Stand at the National Railway Museum on Leeman Road, close to York railway station, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Pick an engine that catches your eye and walk around it. Step back to fit the whole length, then come in close for the details.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to show how huge a whole engine or hall is, and use 1x for general views. Then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for nameplates, wheels, brass and paintwork.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the long lines of the engines straight, and shoot along an engine from a front corner for a sense of depth.
card.best_time: Go earlier in the day if you can, because you'll get fewer people in your shots. The light indoors stays fairly steady, so the crowds matter more than the clock.
card.selfie_here: Find the Gladstone locomotive and stand in front of it, as York's official selfie trail suggests. Use your front camera and try 0.5x to squeeze more of the engine in behind you. The sources don't say which hall it's in, so you may need to ask a member of staff.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine for personal use inside, but follow any signs about restrictions, especially on flash. Opening days and photo areas can vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a nameplate you love, frame it neatly on the gridlines, then take one more shot with a tiny human (you?) standing next to a giant wheel.
card.good_to_know: The museum has been on the site of the old York North locomotive depot since 1975, and it's part of the Science Museum Group. Along with the famous steam engines, it has the front car of a Japanese 0 Series Shinkansen bullet train, one of only two Shinkansen vehicles shown outside Japan. The Station Hall is a Grade II listed former goods station from 1875-77, and it reopened in 2025 after a big refurbishment, so give the building its own photo too.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the National Railway Museum on Leeman Road, close to York railway station, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Pick an engine that catches your eye and walk around it. Step back to fit the whole length, then come in close for the details.

card.hook: Picture a modern York street with shoppers drifting past, and right under your feet is where archaeologists dug up the Viking city of Jórvík. You can't see a single longship, but the old name is right there on the frontage.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right outside the Jorvik Viking Centre entrance on Coppergate. Face the entrance so the whole frontage fills your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the entrance and the street scene. If the pavement is tight, drop to 0.5x to squeeze the whole frontage in, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out a sign or detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the entrance up along one of the vertical lines and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early in the day usually means fewer people in the street, so you get a cleaner shot of the frontage. Overcast or soft light is kind to the building.
card.selfie_here: Stand outside the Jorvik Viking Centre entrance at 19 Coppergate, which is the spot Visit York's selfie trail names. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you want more of the building, and keep the frontage behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed on the ride itself, and rules can differ elsewhere inside, so look for signs and ask staff. Selfie sticks may not be allowed inside, so check with the centre first.
card.challenge: Get one wide shot with a few passers-by for scale, then step in and catch a sign or detail that tells you exactly where you are.
card.good_to_know: York Archaeological Trust created the centre on the dig site, and it opened in 1984. Digs between 1976 and 1981 turned up well-preserved timber buildings, workshops and over 40,000 everyday objects. By October 2022 the centre had welcomed 20 million visitors.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right outside the Jorvik Viking Centre entrance on Coppergate. Face the entrance so the whole frontage fills your screen.

card.hook: Clifford's Tower sits on its grassy mound like a stone cake on a very green cake stand. That lift is a gift for your photo, because the tower stands clear of everything around it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Tower Gardens, on the lawns beneath the tower, and face north-east. The tower rises from its mound with the River Ouse and the obelisk close by in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the tower, the lawn and the obelisk together. Try zoom 0.5x for more river and lawn, or zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a tight shot of the tower on its mound.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sky is doing something nice, because the tower's clean outline against it is the star. If you fancy the roof deck, check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Climb the green slope of the grassy mound and turn so the stone tower is behind you. One local guide calls it a fine backdrop for a cheeky selfie. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it so the tower fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Tower Street to shoot up at the tower with you in front of it, and let them check the view before they snap.
card.rules_and_safety: The steps up the mound are steep, and English Heritage says there are three resting places along the way, so take it at your own pace. Going up the tower to the roof deck is ticketed.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, put the tower on an upper third point, and get two buildings and some river in one shot.
card.good_to_know: The first castle here was a wooden one, built on the orders of William the Conqueror in 1068. Henry III rebuilt the keep in stone in the middle of the 13th century, with an unusual four-lobed (quatrefoil) plan. An explosion in 1684 destroyed the inside, which is why it's a shell today. It's now looked after by English Heritage.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Tower Gardens, on the lawns beneath the tower, and face north-east. The tower rises from its mound with the River Ouse and the obelisk close by in the frame.

card.hook: Everyone calls them the Roman walls, but most of the stone you'll be standing next to went up in the 13th and 14th centuries. Still, they make a lovely grey zigzag to point your phone along.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Station Road and Station Rise, at the steps and platform up to the wall walk. Face the stretch of wall so it fills the foreground, with York Minster's towers rising above the rooftops behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a balanced shot. Try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more wall, or zoom 2x (depending on your phone) to bring the Minster's towers closer above the roofs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the wall along the lower third so it leads your eye to the Minster, and keep the phone level so the battlements don't slope.
card.best_time: One guide recommends sunrise or sunset here. The walls close at dusk, so check the official site before you plan an evening visit.
card.selfie_here: Go up onto the walls opposite The Grand Hotel, reached from the Station Rise and Station Road junction. Guides call it the walls' signature viewpoint, with Lendal Bridge and the Minster in one shot. Use the front camera and keep the Minster over your shoulder. For a different backdrop, try the Museum Gardens entrance, where the original Roman wall and the Multangular Tower stand.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Exhibition Square just below the William Etty statue, to its right, and shoot towards Bootham Bar while you stand by the bar with the walls in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Some wall sections have no inner railings and a drop of about 3 metres, so keep clear of the edge, keep one hand free, and never step backwards while framing a shot. The walls close at dusk, and dogs aren't allowed apart from assistance dogs. Parts may close for repairs, snow or ice, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Get the battlements along the bottom of your frame and both Minster towers peeking over the rooftops, with not a single sloping line in sight.
card.good_to_know: York's walls are the longest town walls in England, and York has more miles of intact wall than any other English city. The first defences here date from around 71 AD, when the Romans built a fort beside the River Ouse. The Victorians later repaired the walls and widened the wall-walk.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Station Road and Station Rise, at the steps and platform up to the wall walk. Face the stretch of wall so it fills the foreground, with York Minster's towers rising above the rooftops behind it.

card.hook: Those pale, formal buildings look like they've been standing guard over York forever, but the museum inside only opened in 1938. The site is much older than that, and it shows in the stonework.
card.stand_here: Walk to Clifford's Tower, then head just south, because York Castle Museum is immediately south of it. The phone icon on the map sits in the middle of the museum site, so stroll a little way across the open space between the old prison buildings until one frontage fills your view.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for a whole building, and try 0.5x if you're close to a long frontage and can't step back. Then move to zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the clock turret, doorways and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building edges up with them, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the pale stone than harsh midday sun. Mornings are also usually quieter, so you'll have an easier time getting a shot without people in it.
card.selfie_here: Stand near the museum entrance with the museum at your back and Clifford's Tower ahead of you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and let the building fill the space over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine for personal use, but some exhibits may have restrictions, and flash is usually discouraged, so look for signs or ask staff. It's a ticketed museum and some parts may be closed at times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots in a row: the whole building from a little way back, the clock turret on the Debtors' Prison, then a close-up of the stonework. Bonus points if the walls stay straight.
card.good_to_know: William the Conqueror first built York Castle here in 1068. The Debtors' Prison went up in 1701-05 using stone from the ruined castle, and the Female Prison followed in the 1780s. The museum's Kirkgate was the first recreated Victorian street of its kind in Britain, and Dick Turpin was held in the Debtors' Prison in the 1730s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to Clifford's Tower, then head just south, because York Castle Museum is immediately south of it. The phone icon on the map sits in the middle of the museum site, so stroll a little way across the open space between the old prison buildings until one frontage fills your view.

The Clifford's Tower spot is a passer-by viewpoint inferred from a photo caption; the tower has a fee and a steep climb, so it is not a casual stop. No page mentioned selfie sticks, so no stick rule is given. Tripod and flash rules are inconsistent between sources and should be checked on arrival.

card.hook: Here's a nice trick: you get a grand old museum and a ruined abbey in one stroll, and the gardens around them are free to enter. The abbey ruins are the real star of your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Museum Gardens, by the Yorkshire Museum, somewhere the St Mary's Abbey ruins are in view, and turn so the ruins are behind your subject. For the museum shot, walk about 90 m east towards the museum and face its front.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for a person or selfie with the ruins behind. Try zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) for a tighter portrait. Switch to zoom 0.5x when you're close to the museum and want its whole front in the picture.
card.make_it_pop: Tap on your subject's face, then slide it a little darker if the pale stone looks washed out, and turn on gridlines to keep things level.
card.best_time: Late afternoon gives you warm light on the old stone. Go early in the morning if you'd like it quieter.
card.selfie_here: Take it in Museum Gardens, by the Yorkshire Museum: use the front camera and keep the abbey ruins over your shoulder. The ruins, not the museum, are the backdrop in this shot, and it's the pose the York selfie trail suggests.
card.rules_and_safety: If you go inside the museum, look for photography signs, as flash may not be allowed.
card.challenge: Get two shots without going indoors: you in front of the ruins, then the museum's front filling the whole picture.
card.good_to_know: William Wilkins designed the museum in a Greek Revival style, and it's Grade I listed. It opened in 1830, which makes it one of the longest-established museums in England. The land came from the old St Mary's Abbey estate, granted to the Yorkshire Philosophical Society on condition that the grounds became botanic gardens. Those gardens are now the Museum Gardens.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Museum Gardens, by the Yorkshire Museum, somewhere the St Mary's Abbey ruins are in view, and turn so the ruins are behind your subject. For the museum shot, walk about 90 m east towards the museum and face its front.

selfie_spots.name: Museum Gardens, by the Yorkshire Museum
selfie_spots.detail: Stand by the Yorkshire Museum inside Museum Gardens. The Abbey ruins, not the museum, are the backdrop in this shot.
selfie_spots.why: Visit York's selfie trail places the visitor beside the museum for a shot with St Mary's Abbey ruins behind, which is the nearest match to the museum in the sources I found.

card.hook: Most people walk past the Merchant Adventurers' Hall looking at the street. The good side is the one facing the river, where old timber, red brick and a garden stack up like layers in one frame.
card.stand_here: Make your way to Piccadilly, opposite the Hall where the street opens onto the river side. The Hall is to the north-east, less than a minute on foot. Face it and let the garden fill the lower part of your picture, with the timber storey and chapel above.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole Hall across its garden. Try zoom 0.5x if the street feels narrow or you want more garden and riverside, and zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the timber and the chapel brickwork.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the timber storey on the upper line and the garden on the lower one, so the building isn't stuck dead centre.
card.best_time: Go when the light is soft, like early morning or late afternoon. You'll also have fewer people wandering through your foreground.
card.selfie_here: Head to the painted red entrance door on Fossgate, right next to the Hairy Fig, and stand in front of it with the door behind you. Use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x if you want more of the doorway in the shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Piccadilly, looking down over the wall at the Hall and its garden, so they can fit the whole scene in with you.
card.rules_and_safety: The views from Piccadilly and Fossgate are from the street. The walled garden and interior are reached through the Hall and may need an entry fee, so check the official site first if you want to photograph inside.
card.challenge: Take a second shot on Fossgate, where the street leads your eye to the gatehouse entrance, and see if you can fit the coat of arms above the doorway in the frame.
card.good_to_know: The Hall stands in the middle of York. The side facing the river is its best-known face, and the view across the garden is the one most often painted and photographed. Fossgate is closed to cars for much of the day, so it's largely pedestrian and easier to stand and line up a shot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Make your way to Piccadilly, opposite the Hall where the street opens onto the river side. The Hall is to the north-east, less than a minute on foot. Face it and let the garden fill the lower part of your picture, with the timber storey and chapel above.

card.hook: Picture a medieval gatehouse sitting right at the end of a road, with towers on both sides and cars driving through it like it's nothing. That's Micklegate Bar, and it's a lot more photogenic than your average roundabout.
card.stand_here: Stand on Blossom Street, on the south side of the street, and face the bar head-on. From here the whole front of the gatehouse sits at the end of the road.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole gatehouse in. If the road and buildings either side crowd the frame, try 2x to tidy it up. Only use 0.5x if you're very close, and keep the bar in the middle so the edges don't stretch it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the arch up with the centre line so the towers stand nice and upright.
card.best_time: There's no special time of day for this one. Just wait for a quiet moment so people and vehicles stay out of the frame. If you're here after dark and the bar is lit, try night mode and rest your phone against a wall or post to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Go to the city-wall path on the city side of the bar, just where it leaves the west edge of the gate. Face down Micklegate into York with the gatehouse behind you, use the front camera, and hold it a little high so the gate fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Blossom Street pavement facing the bar, while you pose in front of the gateway so the whole bar fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Traffic runs through the gate, so keep to the pavement while you frame your shot and never stand in the road. If you plan to walk the wall itself, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get both towers dead level on the gridlines with not a single van in the picture. Patience is the whole game here.
card.good_to_know: Micklegate Bar is one of the four main gatehouses, or 'bars', in York's city walls. In medieval times the gates restricted traffic and were used to collect tolls. The Victorians restored much of the walls, including the battlements, so what you see is a mix of medieval work and later repair.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Blossom Street, on the south side of the street, and face the bar head-on. From here the whole front of the gatehouse sits at the end of the road.

selfie_spots.why: The view down Micklegate into the city is described as best seen from this point on the wall walk, so the gate sits behind you as the backdrop.

card.hook: Picture a square full of people all holding up phones at the same little stone gate, and you're about to join them. There's a good reason: a dark arch, red roofs and York Minster behind it say 'York' in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand in Exhibition Square, outside the bar, below the William Etty statue, on the right of the statue. Face the gate so the arch is in front of you and the Minster rises behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the gate, the red roofs and the Minster together. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the Minster closer behind the arch. Use 0.5x only if you're very close to the gate or want the whole square in the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the arch on the centre line and hold your phone level so the gate doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Morning and golden hour are your best bets. Mid-afternoon sun can be harsh on the stonework.
card.selfie_here: Try Exhibition Square beside the William Etty statue, outside York City Art Gallery. The statue faces the bar across the square, so the gate is close by. Use the front camera, turn so the gate is over your shoulder, and try 0.5x to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the square just below the Etty statue, to its right, while you stand in front of the gate with the Minster beyond.
card.rules_and_safety: A busy road separates the square from the bar, so cross at the traffic lights. The walls are free to walk but may close at dusk, so check the official site on the day.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd and get one shot with the arch totally empty. Bonus points if the Minster is peeking over the top.
card.good_to_know: Bootham Bar is one of the four main gateways, or 'bars', of York's city walls. It once controlled traffic and collected tolls. The walls follow the line of the original Roman defences from around 71 AD, though most of the stonework you see is medieval and Victorian restoration.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Exhibition Square, outside the bar, below the William Etty statue, on the right of the statue. Face the gate so the arch is in front of you and the Minster rises behind it.

card.hook: Picture a row of tall pale arches with nothing behind them but sky, and a flowerbed doing its best to steal the show. That's St Mary's Abbey, and it's a lot more dramatic than a pile of old stones has any right to be.
card.stand_here: Go in by the Museum Street entrance in Museum Gardens, just north of Lendal Bridge. The ruins are about 81 m to the north-east, so face that way and look across the lawns to the arches.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic view, then try 0.5x if you want more arches and flowers in the frame. Switch to 2x or more (depends on your phone) for close-ups of the arches and doorways.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the main arch on one of the lines and let the flowers run along the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Go early, especially in summer, when the gardens are busy. You'll get cleaner pictures with far fewer people wandering through your shot.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Yorkshire Museum in Museum Gardens with the abbey ruins behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the arches, and keep the ruins over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The gardens are free to enter, but check the official site for opening times before you go. After heavy rain, the Hospitium near the river in the same gardens can be surrounded by flood water.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot first, then walk closer and find a doorway to frame like a little window into the past.
card.good_to_know: A church was first founded on this site in 1055, and the abbey was refounded in 1088. The arches you see today come from a rebuilding that began in 1271 and was finished by 1294. At full size the church was about 110 m long, and the abbey closed in 1539 during the dissolution of the monasteries.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go in by the Museum Street entrance in Museum Gardens, just north of Lendal Bridge. The ruins are about 81 m to the north-east, so face that way and look across the lawns to the arches.

card.hook: Walmgate Bar is two photos in one building. The front is all barbican and portcullis, and the back has a timber-framed Elizabethan extension and a coat of arms. Most people only get one of them.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Lawrence Street and Walmgate, by Jenny's Fish & Chips, and face west toward the bar. From there the outer barbican and the archway with its portcullis line up straight down the road.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole barbican and archway in. If a wall or pavement stops you stepping back, try zoom 0.5x and keep the gate in the middle so the edges don't stretch. Then go to zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the portcullis and the coat of arms.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the archway in the centre. Then tap the archway and slide the brightness a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out the stonework.
card.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter on the road and gives softer light, though the junction is busy most of the time. Take a few shots in a row, because cars and people keep drifting through the frame.
card.selfie_here: Climb the steps up to the next section of the city walls beside the bar, then turn back toward it. A walls-trail guide says these steps give an excellent view back to the gate, so it should sit nicely behind you. Use the front camera, and zoom 0.5x if your phone has it for the front camera, and hold it a bit low so the gate stays over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the corner of Lawrence Street outside Jenny's Fish & Chips, facing west, so the whole barbican and gate fill their frame while you pose with the gate behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is one of York's busiest junctions, so use the pedestrian crossing towards the city instead of stepping into traffic to frame a shot. Check the official site before you go for current access to the walls and the gatehouse café.
card.challenge: Get one picture with the gate perfectly upright and not a single car in it. Then see how many tries it takes you.
card.good_to_know: Walmgate Bar is one of the four main gatehouses, or 'bars', on York's city walls. In medieval times these gates restricted traffic and were used to collect tolls. York's walls are the longest town walls in England, mostly dating from the 13th to 14th centuries with Victorian repairs. They are a scheduled monument and a grade I listed structure.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Lawrence Street and Walmgate, by Jenny's Fish & Chips, and face west toward the bar. From there the outer barbican and the archway with its portcullis line up straight down the road.

card.hook: Treasurer's House has a perfectly balanced stone front and a neat gate, so it's the sort of building that makes you feel like a great photographer. The catch is that someone will stroll through the gateway just as you tap the button.
card.stand_here: Stand on Minster Yard, about 40 m south-west of the house, and face north-east so the gate and the house front sit in your frame together. It's not exactly opposite the gate, so walk a little closer if you want a straighter view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the gate and the house front in one shot. If the street feels tight, try zoom 0.5x, but keep the house in the middle so the edges don't stretch. In the garden, zoom 2x or more is lovely for stonework, statues and topiary.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, line the gate up with the centre of the house and keep the phone level so the walls stand up straight.
card.best_time: Morning is a good time for a sunlit house front. It also usually means fewer people in your picture.
card.selfie_here: Try the walled garden (Treasurer's House garden, Minster Yard), near the lawns and stone statues, with the Minster visible beyond. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the landmark fits over your shoulder. The Minster may be your main backdrop here rather than the house, so check on arrival, and check garden access on the day.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Chapter House Street, a few steps from the main entrance, and frame the house front while you pose in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine in the gardens but may be restricted inside the house, so ask at the door or look for signs. Flash is usually not allowed indoors. The house has an admission fee and the garden may not always be free, so check opening times on the official site on the day.
card.challenge: Get the gate dead centre on your gridlines with nobody walking through it. Bonus points for patience.
card.good_to_know: The first Treasurer of the Minster was appointed in 1091, though little of the original house survives. The Young family added the symmetrical front in the early 17th century, which is the look you see today. The house sits on a Roman road, which is behind a well-known ghost story about marching Roman soldiers in the cellar.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Minster Yard, about 40 m south-west of the house, and face north-east so the gate and the house front sit in your frame together. It's not exactly opposite the gate, so walk a little closer if you want a straighter view.

card.hook: Picture a long lane of timber-fronted buildings with York Minster poking up over the rooftops at the far end. That's Stonegate, and the photo is practically ready-made.
card.stand_here: Stand at the edge of St Helen's Square, at the mouth of Stonegate. Face north-east and look straight down the street towards the Minster.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole street in. Then try zoom 2x to bring the Minster a bit closer.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines and keep the phone level so the building fronts stay upright.
card.best_time: Go early in the day or later in the evening, when there are usually fewer people. If a few figures wander into the shot, they help show how big the street is.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the Stonegate pavement beside the entrance to Coffee Yard, under the red devil carving. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt up a little so the devil and the street behind you both fit.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the St Helen's Square end of Stonegate while you walk a little way up the street, so they can frame you with the buildings around you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stonegate is a public street. If you plan to go into any building, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Take a shot where every building front is perfectly upright and the Minster sits neatly at the top of the street, then give yourself a point for each person you can leave out.
card.good_to_know: Stonegate is one of York's best-known streets for a photograph. Its unusual old name was Whip-ma-whop-ma-gate, and you can pose beside a street sign that carries it. For a second angle, walk up to Minster Yard, where the towers sit close above the buildings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the edge of St Helen's Square, at the mouth of Stonegate. Face north-east and look straight down the street towards the Minster.

card.hook: Here's a funny one: the worst place to photograph Lendal Bridge is on Lendal Bridge, because you're standing on it and it vanishes from your frame. Step back and let the river do the work.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ouse Bridge, near the Guildhall, and face back up the river toward Lendal Bridge. You'll get the river in front of you, the bridge in the middle distance, and the Guildhall and moored boats at the sides.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit in the river, the bridge and the buildings beside it. Then try 2x to bring the bridge closer. Save 0.5x for when you want lots of water and sky, but the bridge will look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the bridge on a third, and keep the phone level so the bridge doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go at sunset or blue hour, when the river can pick up the bridge and the sky colour. If it's dusk, switch on night mode and hold still while it captures.
card.selfie_here: Climb up onto the City Walls by Station Rise, opposite the Grand Hotel. Use the front camera at 0.5x and the Minster and Lendal Bridge can both fit behind you in one shot.
card.ask_someone: Along Dame Judy Dench Walk, the riverside path down to the bridge, ask a passer-by to frame the whole bridge with you in it.
card.rules_and_safety: Ouse Bridge and the riverside are open public places, but check for closures or works before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the pedestrians and boats, then get a shot with the river running straight up to the bridge and nobody in the way.
card.good_to_know: Lendal Bridge opened in 1863 and was designed by Thomas Page, who also designed London's Westminster Bridge. The first attempt, begun in 1860, collapsed during construction and five workmen were killed. Before any bridge, a rope ferry crossed here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ouse Bridge, near the Guildhall, and face back up the river toward Lendal Bridge. You'll get the river in front of you, the bridge in the middle distance, and the Guildhall and moored boats at the sides.

card.hook: Monk Bar looms over Goodramgate like a stone bouncer, and the street is so narrow you'll find yourself shuffling backwards to fit it all in.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Goodramgate pavement, on the city side inside the walls, and face the gatehouse from the Goodramgate end. You'll be looking straight at its inner face, with the arches, shields and upper storeys.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole gatehouse fits in the narrow street, then try 1x for a more natural look. Zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the shields and the upper storeys.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the gatehouse centred and hold your phone as level as you can so the tower doesn't lean back, then tap the stonework and drag the slider to make it slightly darker so the sky doesn't wash out the gate.
card.best_time: One guide says the walls close at dusk, so go earlier in the day if you want to walk the wall. Check the official opening times before you set off.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the Goodramgate pavement, facing into the street so the gate is behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to squeeze more of the tower in over your shoulder, and check the background on the ground, because it's a tight, busy street.
card.ask_someone: Walk about 15 metres past the portcullis and photograph back at the front of the bar, or hand your phone to a passer-by there and step into the shot (if the pavement is busy, use the quiet alleyway nearby).
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement and watch for traffic and other people before you step back to frame a shot. The stairwell in and out of Monk Bar is narrow with a low ceiling, and the wall-walk steps are steep, so take care.
card.challenge: Find the shields on the upper storeys and see how many you can fit in one shot without the tower leaning.
card.good_to_know: Monk Bar is one of the four main gatehouses, or 'bars', in York's city walls, and gatehouses like this once slowed traffic and collected tolls. Much of what you see dates from the 13th and 14th centuries, tidied up by the Victorians, who widened the wall-walk and rebuilt many of the battlements. York has more miles of intact wall than any other city in England. The attraction inside the gate was closed when we last checked and may not reopen, so plan to enjoy Monk Bar from the outside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Goodramgate pavement, on the city side inside the walls, and face the gatehouse from the Goodramgate end. You'll be looking straight at its inner face, with the arches, shields and upper storeys.

card.hook: Here's a twist: the best view of Ouse Bridge isn't from the bridge, because you can't see a bridge while standing on it. Head down to the water instead and the whole thing opens up.
card.stand_here: Stand on King's Staith, on the east (south-east) bank below the bridge, by the pub terrace. Go down the steps to the terrace, then turn around and face the bridge across the water.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the bridge from the terrace. Try 0.5x if you want more terrace and water in front, and keep the bridge towards the middle of the picture. If your phone has 2x, it's good for the arch and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the arch on the upper third, with the water and terrace in the lower two thirds, then tap the bridge and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Pick a day when the river is low, because the terrace can flood when the Ouse rises. Check the ground from the top of the steps before you go down.
card.selfie_here: York's selfie trail picks the middle of the bridge on Bridge Street. Stop halfway across and take it looking down towards the Old Bonding Warehouse, with King's Staith, Cumberland House and Queens Staith in frame. Use the front camera at 0.5x to fit more riverside in. The bridge is the spot rather than the backdrop here, so it won't be behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from the riverside near the Kings Arms pub on King's Staith, with Ouse Bridge in view.
card.rules_and_safety: The terrace can flood when the river is high, so look at the ground before you go down and stay back from the water's edge.
card.challenge: Get three layers in one shot: the pub terrace up close, the river in the middle, and the big arch behind.
card.good_to_know: The Vikings built a wooden bridge here, and it collapsed in 1154 under a crowd waiting to greet St William of York. In 1367 the stone bridge that replaced it carried what were probably the first public toilets in England. The bridge you see today was designed by Peter Atkinson the younger, finished in 1821, and is Grade II listed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on King's Staith, on the east (south-east) bank below the bridge, by the pub terrace. Go down the steps to the terrace, then turn around and face the bridge across the water.

selfie_spots.why: Visit York's selfie trail names this as its best view of the River Ouse, with Kings Staith, Cumberland House and Queens Staith also in frame. The bridge itself is the spot, not the backdrop, so the landmark is not behind the visitor.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with Ouse Bridge directly behind the visitor. The only named selfie spot (Visit York) is on the bridge looking away from it, so I kept it as the best option but it does not meet the 'landmark behind them' brief. The Kings Arms riverbank spot is for a passer-by photo, and its sources are a panorama page and a general guide; neither gives exact standing points. The York360 page also describes a view from Lendal Bridge towards Ouse Bridge, but it is a photo caption, not a selfie guide, so I did not list it. No page I found states selfie stick or tripod rules, and no safety point about this bridge appeared, so those fields are empty.
